items.title: Victor Rendon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Tito Puente had his mambos... I saw the connection between Stan Kenton, Woody Herman, and Tito Puente, and Machito.

ctx.x: And maybe one other tune. But when you’re playing for dancers who know what they’re doing that’s — tempos seem extremely important. What distinguishes a mambo from a cha cha?

Yes. It took me a long time to internalize that. Because we have terms like mambo. We have cha cha cha. We have son son montuno. Guaracha. What is all this? And a lot of it is the same rhythm but at a slower tempo. Like a mambo might be here [scats]. But then if you slow it down [scats] then it becomes a son montuno. It just feels differently. Again the word mambo is used very loosely. Tito Puente had his mambos, like what we were doing during rehearsal yesterday. But then Perez Prado [scats], that was a mambo…
You said something about these terms get confusing over the years and you mentioned the rumba.

items.title: Victor Rendon interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 12, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: It’s an album that Tito Puente did with Mongo Santamaria, Patato and some other percussionists and a bass player.

ctx.x: It’s an album that Tito Puente did with Mongo Santamaria, Patato and some other percussionists and a bass player. [Scats] Then they would solo around that. So that’s a possibility. I haven’t thought about it. You just gave me the idea.
